findings.title: Case-sensitive email lookup allows bypassing blocked emails
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` queries `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` without normalizing the case of `email` (e.g., via `Email.downcase(email)`), and `BlockedEmail` does not normalize `email` before saving either. In PostgreSQL, `=` on `varchar` is case-sensitive, and `User.new_from_params` does not downcase `params[:email]` before running validations. As a result, a blocked address like `bad@spammer.com` can be bypassed simply by signing up with `Bad@spammer.com`.

findings.title: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` mutates match statistics every time validation runs
findings.body: `EmailValidator` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` during standard ActiveRecord validation, and `should_block?` increments `match_count` and updates `last_match_at` in the database on every call. In `UsersController#create`, `user.valid?` is called on line 168 and `user.save` (which runs validations again) is called on line 172. For an email with `action_type == :do_nothing` (or whenever validations are invoked multiple times during a request), `match_count` will be incremented multiple times for a single signup attempt.

findings.title: `change_email` does not check `EmailValidator` / `BlockedEmail` before sending confirmation email
findings.body: In `UsersController#change_email`, an `EmailToken` is created and an authorization email is enqueued without validating the new address against `EmailValidator` or `BlockedEmail` (unless `EmailToken` itself runs `EmailValidator`, which is only added to `User` in this PR). Even if `EmailToken.confirm` later fails when updating `user.email`, the system still sends an email to the blocked address and only fails at confirmation time.
